person.name: Dong Hwi Kim
person.affiliation: Mechanical Engineering & Electrical and Computer Engineering · Seoul National University
person.intro: I am an undergraduate at Seoul National University studying Mechanical Engineering and Electrical and Computer Engineering. My interests lie in how machines perceive the physical world and turn that understanding into useful behavior.
person.bio: At the RPM Robotics Lab, I work with Prof. Ayoung Kim on 3D Gaussian Splatting for SLAM: estimating camera motion while building a 3D map. At the AIDAS Lab, my collaboration with Prof. Jaeyoung Do uses reconstructed scenes and robot kinematics to generate visual training data for robot learning. A first-author manuscript based on my ongoing research is currently in preparation.
approach: Projects and competitions have given me hands-on experience in AI, robotics, and control, including connecting learned models with software and physical systems. Lab research is teaching me a complementary discipline: formulating research questions, designing experiments, and critically evaluating results.

An international-school education and four years in China exposed me early to different ways of learning. Later, serving as a Korean–English interpreter at the ROK–U.S. Combined Forces Command meant working across languages and military cultures. These experiences shape how I learn and collaborate: listen carefully, ask when assumptions differ, and stay willing to revise my own.

Robotics and 3D vision are my current focus. My curiosity also extends to problems in other fields—especially when solving them could help people, or when the challenge of making an idea work offers something new to learn. I welcome conversations with people who bring different questions, tools, and perspectives.

research.title: Gaussian Scene Representations for SLAM
research.image_alt: Conceptual illustration of camera observations, Gaussian scene representation, and camera trajectory; not an experimental result
research.summary: Building 3D maps from moving cameras, with an emphasis on geometric consistency and how mapping computation is spent.
research.role: Research on 3D Gaussian Splatting mapping, optimization, and geometric consistency at RPM Robotics Lab.

sections.heading: A useful map must explain more than its training images
sections.body: 3D Gaussian Splatting represents a scene as many small, oriented 3D elements that can be rendered into an image. My research asks how that representation can support mapping: which observations to optimize, how to use geometric evidence, and how to spend computation where the reconstruction still needs work.

sections.heading: One concrete engineering problem: coordinate consistency
sections.body: In my public Aria-to-3DGS pipeline, stereo-inertial tracking exports camera poses, map points, and observations into the same raw map frame before conversion to a reconstruction dataset. Mixing those map points with a separately normalized trajectory would silently break their spatial relationship. Sparse depth targets, consistency checks, and ablation tools make this interface explicit.

sections.heading: What I am investigating now
sections.body: Current experiments examine how optimization effort is allocated across views and how depth or free-space evidence can constrain spurious geometry. These are research questions under evaluation. The work is ongoing, and I am preparing a manuscript; results across scenes and computational trade-offs still need broader validation.

technical_notes.heading: Research direction
technical_notes.body: This ongoing project investigates the use of 3D Gaussian Splatting in simultaneous localization and mapping. The goal is to connect camera motion estimation with a 3D representation of the surrounding scene.

technical_notes.heading: Current status
technical_notes.body: The manuscript is in preparation. Further method details, experimental results, and publication information will be shared as the work progresses.

technical_notes.heading: Public implementation thread
technical_notes.body: The Aria-to-3DGS repository contains tracking exports, dataset conversion, sparse-depth target generation, consistency checks, and mapping ablation scripts. It is a supporting pipeline within the broader mapping research.

research.card_role: 3DGS mapping research; experiments and manuscript in progress.

research.title: Multi-View Demonstration Augmentation
research.image_alt: An FR3 manipulation episode rendered from three camera viewpoints using Gaussian scene assets
research.summary: Turning workcell captures and robot motion into reusable 3D assets that render the same manipulation episode from multiple cameras.
research.role: Responsible for the 3DGS data augmentation module within a larger collaborative dataset project.

sections.heading: My part: making reconstructed scenes reusable
sections.body: I develop the 3DGS augmentation module within a larger robotic dataset collaboration. The module connects captured appearance to calibrated cameras, robot link geometry, and demonstration motion. It builds on RoboSplat and SplatSim; my focus is the reconstruction, alignment, asset preparation, rendering, and validation needed for the FR3 workcell.

sections.heading: Looking aligned is not the same as being metrically aligned
sections.body: A soft Gaussian silhouette can make an incorrectly scaled robot look plausible. I therefore use calibration and distances between rigid robot parts to check scale against the robot CAD model. Registration is refined on opaque Gaussian cores with scale fixed. This makes the alignment decision depend on physical dimensions.

figure.alt: Repository figure comparing robot length-ruler errors and Gaussian-core distances before and after scale correction
figure.caption: Scale checks compare rigid-part distances against CAD. The figure reports the repository’s reference capture, rather than a result across all scenes.

sections.heading: Motion, appearance, and object state must agree
sections.body: Each Gaussian belongs to a robot link. Inverse forward kinematics brings those assets into a reusable reference pose; forward kinematics then animates them along a trajectory. Explicit attachment and release rules keep objects connected to the gripper at the right times. Camera visibility and object-pose continuity are checked before an episode is accepted.

figure.alt: Four rendered stages of the same FR3 cube-stacking episode
figure.caption: A generated episode progresses through approach, grasp, and stacking. The montage illustrates the kinematic replay; it is not a physical policy-success trial.

sections.heading: Turn visible failures into explicit checks
sections.body: Missing cube bottoms, a hazy tabletop, and objects disappearing from the wrist view exposed different pipeline failures. The module uses targeted asset repairs and numerical acceptance checks rather than relying only on a convincing render. The next research question is how such generated data affects downstream robot learning; generation checks alone do not answer it.

research.card_role: Developing the 3DGS augmentation module in a larger dataset collaboration.

technical_notes.heading: My scope within the collaboration
technical_notes.body: My contribution to the broader robotic dataset collaboration is the 3D Gaussian Splatting augmentation module. It turns workcell captures and demonstrations into reusable scene assets that can be reposed and rendered as synchronized training views. The collaboration and manuscript remain in progress.

technical_notes.heading: Metric scale and registration
technical_notes.body: A scene can look convincing and still have the wrong metric scale. The pipeline uses ChArUco calibration and pose-invariant lengths between rigid robot parts to check scale against the URDF. Registration is then refined using high-opacity Gaussian cores with scale held fixed. This avoids letting a diffuse reconstruction shell determine the robot’s dimensions.

technical_notes.heading: Connecting appearance to kinematics
technical_notes.body: Gaussians are assigned to the nearest CAD link surface. Applying the inverse of each link’s forward-kinematics transform converts the posed robot geometry into canonical link assets, which can then be reposed along a demonstration. An explicit kinematic contract defines object attachment and release, keeping rendered appearance, joint motion, and object motion in a consistent coordinate system.

technical_notes.heading: Repairing capture-specific failure modes
technical_notes.body: Static captures miss cube bottoms, and a low-texture tabletop can reconstruct as haze. The pipeline merges only missing cube geometry from a rolled capture and replaces tabletop fog with a sheet on the calibrated plane, bounded by the measured table footprint. These are targeted scene repairs, not an assumption that novel-view quality alone guarantees usable manipulation geometry.

technical_notes.heading: Validation before dataset generation
technical_notes.body: The module checks geometry, forward-kinematics round trips, grasp state, object-pose continuity, wrist-camera visibility, and black frames before accepting generated episodes. Resumable stages and immutable dataset shards separate long generation jobs from release validation. The engineering focus is to turn visible rendering defects into measurable acceptance criteria; dataset-generation checks do not by themselves establish downstream policy success.

at_glance.text: Collecting robot demonstrations is costly, and a good-looking reconstruction may have the wrong scale or motion.

at_glance.label: The approach
at_glance.text: Align reconstructed assets to the real robot, animate them with its kinematics, and render calibrated views.

at_glance.label: Outcome / status
at_glance.text: A working scene-generation and validation pipeline; the broader robot-learning collaboration remains ongoing.

projects.title: Autonomous Object-Collecting Robot
projects.image_alt: Team 7's autonomous mecanum-wheel robot in the competition arena
projects.summary: An autonomous robot that recognizes, collects, and delivers target objects during a 180-second match.
projects.role: Perception and model training, together with Jinyong Jun.

sections.heading: The mechanism shaped the software
sections.body: The collector holds three objects and has no capture actuator: moving forward collects, while reversing releases. The team therefore used a fixed sweep route with live target decisions and planned returns for delivery. Braking and turning were calibrated as part of that route. A small corrective move could cost time or lose the load.

figure.alt: Official team repository diagram showing the object grid, storage corner, and robot start corner
figure.caption: The arena separates the start and storage corners. Target recognition must lead to a collection and delivery plan within the match clock.

sections.heading: My contribution: perception that motion can use
sections.body: I worked on perception and model training with Jinyong Jun. The two cameras look outward so objects can be observed as the robot passes. Their detections are expressed in a shared forward-bearing convention and sent together to navigation. This gives the planner visual evidence it can combine with position and target rules, rather than asking the detector to make the whole collection decision.

sections.heading: The integration lesson: accuracy has a time budget
sections.body: A moving robot sees each object for a limited time. Model latency, camera reliability, detection thresholds, and vehicle speed therefore have to work together. The code includes on-device model benchmarks and camera-freeze checks. The team finished second, scoring 70 points in each final run; the linked videos show the competition behavior.

technical_notes.heading: The engineering problem
technical_notes.body: The robot had 180 seconds to find, collect, and deliver two target classes announced at match time. A Jetson Orin Nano ran perception and navigation on a four-wheel mecanum chassis. The key mechanical constraint was a passive, three-object basket: driving forward captured an object, while reversing released it. That made motion planning, stopping, and perception part of the same collection problem.

technical_notes.heading: From software commands to wheel motion
technical_notes.body: The Jetson sent body-velocity commands over a 115200-baud USB serial link to an ESP32, which commanded four JGB37-520 geared DC motors through DRV8871 drivers. The host interface explicitly converted its forward/right/yaw convention to the chassis axes and reapplied per-wheel feed-forward and encoder-direction calibration after connecting. Motion commands carried a duration and auto-stopped at the controller. The hot path sent commands without waiting for an acknowledgement, avoiding serial round-trip delays in the control loop.

technical_notes.heading: Control choices driven by the mechanism
technical_notes.body: The team used a fixed sweep route with live collection decisions. LiDAR wall fitting supplied pose; an IMU integrated yaw to terminate calibrated turn pulses. Lateral moves used LiDAR feedback by default because the documented timed-strafe calibration left 4–7 cm error. Stops used a calibrated reverse-braking pulse, with a useful speed range around 42–57 cm/s. Cruise was therefore set near 44 cm/s rather than pushed toward the motor limit. Route corrections also had to respect the basket’s tendency to release its load during backward travel.

technical_notes.heading: My focus: perception that navigation can use
technical_notes.body: I worked on perception and model training with Jinyong Jun. Two outward-angled USB cameras let the system observe objects beside the route without stopping to face them. The YOLO instance-segmentation node combined both cameras into one UDP message and reprojected horizontal detections into a common forward-facing bearing. Navigation then applied confidence, range-normalized mask-area, bearing, and grid-cell ownership gates. This separated visual evidence from the decision to collect a target.

technical_notes.heading: What the integration makes clear
technical_notes.body: A detector’s offline accuracy is only one part of a usable robot. At the documented scan speed, an object could appear in only two or three inference frames, so demanding many repeated detections could reject real targets. The repository includes an Orin benchmark for model latency and a frame-freeze check for each camera. The engineering lesson is to choose the model, observation gates, and vehicle speed together, and to debug raw camera frames alongside motion logs.

technical_notes.heading: Competition validation
technical_notes.body: Team 7 finished second with 140/200 points across two final runs, collecting three shape targets and two fruit targets per run. The repository includes run videos and documents the calibration limits of the competition prototype.

projects.title: Accelerated MRI Reconstruction
projects.image_alt: Team MRI reconstruction framework using brain and knee experts with Feature VarNet and FI VarNet
projects.summary: Reconstructing brain and knee MRI images from undersampled measurements using learned models tied to the acquisition process.

sections.heading: Why a plausible image is not enough
sections.body: MRI reconstruction is an inverse problem: the model sees a partial measurement of the image it must recover. Feature VarNet and FI VarNet couple learned features with the acquisition model and data-consistency operations. That structure keeps the reconstruction connected to the acquired signal.

sections.heading: Specialize the model, make the routing explicit
sections.body: Brain and knee scans, and 4× versus 8× acceleration, create different input conditions. The team trained experts for these settings. The inference code identifies anatomy from coil count and acceleration from the sampling mask. The routing follows the challenge data conventions rather than a learned gating network.

sections.heading: The engineering work extends beyond the architecture
sections.body: DeepSpeed, activation checkpointing, resumable training, MRI-aware augmentation, and checkpoint conversion make the models practical to train and reuse. Weight averaging produces one model; prediction ensembling runs multiple models. Keeping those choices separate makes the inference-cost trade-off clear. Team 2rm1000 placed third in the 2025 challenge.

gallery.caption: Official announcement for the 2025 competition.

technical_notes.heading: Measurement-consistent reconstruction
technical_notes.body: The input is undersampled multi-coil k-space, so plausible appearance alone is insufficient: a reconstruction must remain tied to the acquired measurements. The Feature VarNet and FI VarNet implementations estimate coil sensitivities and combine learned updates with data-consistency operations. FI VarNet also includes image-domain cascades. The design couples a learned image prior to the MRI acquisition model.

technical_notes.heading: Specialization with explicit routing
technical_notes.body: Brain and knee scans at 4× and 8× acceleration present different reconstruction conditions. The team trained specialized experts for these cases. At inference, coil count identifies the anatomy and the sampling mask determines acceleration, providing a deterministic route to the appropriate model.

technical_notes.heading: Making the training pipeline practical
technical_notes.body: The repository provides DeepSpeed-based training, activation-checkpointing configuration, resumable checkpoints, and conversion of distributed checkpoint state into FP32 model weights. MRI-aware augmentation and a warmup/cosine schedule support training. These pieces matter because a useful reconstruction architecture must also fit the available memory and survive interrupted experiments.

technical_notes.heading: Two different forms of averaging
technical_notes.body: Checkpoint averaging combines compatible parameter tensors into one model; prediction ensembling instead executes separate models and averages their reconstructions. The averaging utility checks parameter names and shapes, while the inference path supports expert-specific model pairs. Keeping these mechanisms separate makes the inference-cost trade-off explicit: weight averaging does not add another model forward pass.

technical_notes.heading: Result and engineering takeaway
technical_notes.body: Team 2rm1000, with Jinseok Choi, placed third and received a KRW 2,500,000 team prize. The submission brought together measurement-aware models, anatomy-specific inference, and reusable checkpoints in a complete reconstruction pipeline.

at_glance.label: The approach

projects.title: Chronological Ordering of Shuffled Images
projects.image_alt: Diagram of mapping frame-order views into a common coordinate system for Random4 inference
projects.summary: Recovering the chronological order of four shuffled video frames from images and a sentence, with an output that is always a valid ordering.

sections.heading: Make correctness part of the output interface
sections.body: Free-form answers can repeat a frame, omit one, or confuse an ordered list with per-input ranks. The team instead scores all 24 valid permutations using pairwise comparisons and chronological-slot evidence. The decoder guarantees a valid ordering format, although the predicted chronology can still be wrong.

sections.heading: Average evidence only after matching frame identities
sections.body: The same image can appear in a different input position in each test view. Before averaging scores, the implementation maps them to the original frame identities. Otherwise, apparently compatible tensor positions would refer to different images. Tests check those mappings and the final submission format.

sections.heading: Keep the official result reproducible
sections.body: The final adapter averages nine LoRA snapshots into one adapter, without adding a forward pass. Random4 inference still evaluates four input orderings. The official final-selected private score is 0.91463 and the team placed eighth. Later crop-based inference experiments are documented separately from the competition result.

projects.thumbnail_alt: Official blue AI symbol of SNU AI Challenge

technical_notes.heading: A structured output contract
technical_notes.body: Given a sentence and four shuffled frames, the system must return each input frame’s chronological rank. Chronological sequence and per-input rank are inverse permutations; confusing them can invalidate an otherwise correct prediction. The implementation explicitly converts between the two representations and formats the submission through a shared utility.

technical_notes.heading: Reasoning with a constrained decoder
technical_notes.body: The Qwen3.5-27B model uses LoRA adaptation and structured readouts: six frame-pair comparisons and four chronological slots. Their evidence scores the 24 possible orders, and exhaustive decoding selects one valid permutation. This gives the output a useful guarantee—each frame appears exactly once—rather than depending on free-form text to obey the task schema.

technical_notes.heading: Aggregating views in the same coordinates
technical_notes.body: Random4 inference evaluates four input-image orderings. Before averaging raw logits, each view is mapped back to the original frame identities; otherwise the same output position would refer to different images in different views. One decoder then operates on the combined evidence. The repository tests permutation mappings and validates the final submission schema.

technical_notes.heading: Accuracy without another inference ensemble
technical_notes.body: The final-selected Exp43 adapter averages nine language-LoRA snapshots from the same training trajectory in CPU float32. It remains one adapter at inference, so this parameter-space averaging adds no forward passes. Temporal-gap supervision and local hard-negative ranking belong to training. Crop-based test-time augmentation is documented separately as post-competition work.

technical_notes.heading: Result and engineering takeaway
technical_notes.body: GeekSeek finished eighth overall. The repository records 0.91463 as the official final-selected private score; the higher late Crop-TTA score is not an official competition result. The main engineering lesson is that representation contracts, aggregation coordinates, and reproducible artifact selection are as consequential as the model choice.

projects.title: Physics-Guided Wind Power Prediction
projects.image_alt: Zephyr Analytics team cover for the 2025 Wind Power Prediction Competition
projects.summary: Predicting hourly wind-farm generation with a physical power curve, learned error corrections, and an optimized ensemble.
projects.role: Model architecture design and hyperparameter optimization.

sections.heading: Divide the problem between physics and learning
sections.body: A turbine’s power curve provides a physically meaningful starting point. Weather-derived features, including air-density estimation, support that baseline. A residual model then learns the difference between the baseline and observed generation, leaving the ensemble to combine complementary predictions.

sections.heading: My contribution: architecture and optimization
sections.body: I worked on model architecture design and hyperparameter optimization. The team combined the hybrid forecast with Ridge Regression and Random Forest predictions and tuned parameters and ensemble weights with Optuna. Derrick Junsu Lee led machine learning and testing; Hyunseung Lee handled preprocessing and feature engineering.

sections.heading: Assess the forecast in its operating context
sections.body: The team placed third among 270 teams. The presentation reports 19.34% normalized mean absolute error (NMAE) and a 22.09% settlement revenue rate under the competition rule. The site-wise distributions below provide context for the aggregate scores. These are team-reported competition results, not a claim about deployment performance.

technical_notes.heading: Two objectives for an operational forecast
technical_notes.body: The competition required hourly generation forecasts for Gyeongju, Yangyang, and Yeongdeok. Prediction error and settlement revenue describe different aspects of usefulness, so the project reported both. A forecast that looks numerically close must still be evaluated under the competition’s economic scoring rule.

technical_notes.heading: Let physics explain the baseline
technical_notes.body: The team used a physical power curve and weather-derived features, including air-density estimation informed by the Arden–Buck equation. This gives the model a physical starting point: weather conditions imply an expected generation level. A residual LightGBM model then corrects the baseline’s remaining error instead of making the entire mapping depend on a single unconstrained predictor.

technical_notes.heading: My contribution: architecture and optimization
technical_notes.body: I worked on model architecture design and hyperparameter optimization. The team combined the hybrid prediction with Ridge Regression and Random Forest models and used Optuna for tuning, including ensemble weights. Derrick Junsu Lee led machine learning and testing, while Hyunseung Lee handled preprocessing and feature engineering.

technical_notes.heading: Validation and engineering takeaway
technical_notes.body: Zephyr Analytics placed third among 270 teams, with reported NMAE of 19.34% and settlement revenue rate of 22.09%. The site-wise distributions in the evaluation slide help contextualize the aggregate result. The key design lesson is to divide the problem between a physical baseline, learned error correction, and the operational evaluation criterion. These details are drawn from the supplied team slides; no public implementation repository is linked.

projects.title: Face-Tracking Pan–Tilt Camera
projects.image_alt: Sunflower-inspired face-tracking camera device with a yellow phone mount and white circular base
projects.summary: A two-axis camera mount that detects a face and adjusts its pan and tilt to keep the subject in frame.

sections.heading: The algorithm has to move a physical assembly
sections.body: The team combined a Raspberry Pi, camera, two servos, infrared receiver, and a ball-transfer support. The support distributes the load and reduces friction. The software then has to translate an image-space target into motion the pan–tilt mechanism can execute.

figure.alt: Exploded hardware diagram of the pan–tilt filming device
figure.caption: The assembly links camera framing to the mount’s two mechanical axes.

sections.heading: Pixels become pulse widths through an explicit controller
sections.body: The largest face supplies a center point. Its normalized offset drives incremental pan and tilt commands, with angle limits and a calibrated pulse-width mapping. Although the source contains derivative terms, their gains are zero in the final code. The implemented visual controller therefore uses proportional feedback.

sections.heading: A usable prototype includes the operator
sections.body: A separate thread handles infrared commands while the vision loop runs. The operator can switch modes, move either axis, and stop the device. The prototype won the HD Hyundai Mechatronics Grand Prize. The demos show its behavior; quantitative tracking-error and settling-time results are not supplied.

projects.credit: Shared project photographs and diagrams are reproduced from teammate Seunghun Oh’s project page. Project descriptions are adapted for this joint team project.

technical_notes.heading: The mechanism and the control objective
technical_notes.body: A solo creator needs the subject to stay framed while the camera moves smoothly enough to remain usable. The team combined a Raspberry Pi, a wide-view camera, two pan–tilt servos, an infrared receiver, and a ball-transfer support. The support reduces friction and distributes the assembly’s load; the two axes provide horizontal and vertical reframing.

technical_notes.heading: From pixels to actuator commands
technical_notes.body: The final program uses Picamera2 and OpenCV’s Haar-cascade detector, selecting the largest detected face. Its horizontal and vertical offsets from the image center are normalized by frame dimensions and converted into incremental servo-angle commands. pigpio maps those commands to servo pulse widths with an explicit offset, pulse cap, and angle limits.

technical_notes.heading: What the controller actually implements
technical_notes.body: The source contains proportional and derivative terms, but both derivative gains are set to zero in final.py. The checked-in implementation therefore acts as proportional image-error feedback, rather than demonstrating a tuned PID controller. The stored angle is the commanded angle; there is no separate measured joint-angle feedback in this program. This distinction separates visual feedback from the servo’s internal position regulation.

technical_notes.heading: Manual control and device state
technical_notes.body: A separate thread reads LIRC’s irw output so remote commands can switch automatic/manual operation, move either axis, stop, or exit while the vision loop continues. An LED indicates face detection. On shutdown, the program terminates the remote process, stops the camera, and disables servo pulses. This joins the tracking algorithm to an actual device interaction loop.

technical_notes.heading: Result and engineering takeaway
technical_notes.body: The team received the 2024 HD Hyundai Mechatronics Competition Grand Prize and a KRW 3,000,000 team prize. The project’s engineering value lies in connecting camera coordinates, control gains, calibrated pulse widths, mechanical support, and user input. The linked demos show prototype behavior; the repository does not supply quantitative tracking-error or settling-time measurements.

projects.title: Period-Aware Time-Series Forecasting
projects.image_alt: Original presentation slide showing the TaXer periodic feature extraction and cross-attention architecture
projects.summary: Testing whether explicit periodic or convolutional features help a transformer forecast weather and retail-sales sequences.

sections.heading: The question is where to combine two models
sections.body: Rather than averaging independent forecasts, the team placed a temporal feature extractor inside the forecasting model. TaXer detects dominant periods with FFT and models within-period and across-period variation. WaXer uses dilated causal convolutions as a different temporal prior.

sections.heading: The interface is a learnable representation
sections.body: A linear projection matches the extracted features to the transformer’s embedding dimension. The original sequence is embedded into variable-wise patches, while the extracted features provide cross-attention context. Keeping shapes and normalization explicit lets the two representations interact and returns predictions at the original scale.

sections.heading: Read the result with its experimental scope
sections.body: The supplied report evaluates weather and Sticker Sales data and includes model-size comparisons. Its main Sticker Sales table reports TaXer MSE of 0.1569 versus 0.1647 for TimeXer. These are results under the course-project setup. The report and slides provide the experimental context.

figure.alt: Team presentation comparing ground-truth and predicted time-series traces
figure.caption: Forecast traces from the course presentation provide a qualitative view alongside the reported error metrics.

technical_notes.heading: The design question
technical_notes.body: Can a transformer benefit from a feature extractor that explicitly captures temporal structure? The team compared TaXer, which uses TimesNet-style periodic features, with WaXer, which uses WaveNet-style dilated causal convolutions. Weather and Sticker Sales sequences provide different tests of the same integration idea.

technical_notes.heading: Connecting two models at the right interface
technical_notes.body: TaXer detects dominant periods through FFT-based TimesNet features, then uses a learned linear projection to match the transformer’s embedding dimension. Variable-wise patch embeddings provide the endogenous sequence, while the extracted features are broadcast as cross-attention context. The encoder’s global token queries that context. This is feature-level integration, rather than averaging two independent forecasts.

technical_notes.heading: An alternative temporal prior
technical_notes.body: WaXer replaces the periodic feature extractor with dilated causal convolutions while keeping the projection and transformer integration pattern. The two variants let the team compare explicit periodic structure with a convolutional receptive field. Input/output shapes and per-variable normalization are handled explicitly so forecasts can be returned at the original scale.

technical_notes.heading: Evaluation and engineering takeaway
technical_notes.body: The supplied report compares models on global weather, Korean weather, and Sticker Sales, including model-size ablations. Its main Sticker comparison reports TaXer MSE of 0.1569 versus 0.1647 for TimeXer. These are course-project results under the reported setup. The useful engineering question is how representation choice, model capacity, and inference cost interact.

technical_notes.heading: Team and materials
technical_notes.body: This SNU Introduction to Deep Learning project was completed by Donghwi Kim, Jinwoo Seo, Hyeonseop Shin, and Manyoung Han. The code, report, and presentation provide the implementation and experimental context; the work is presented as a course project.
